hints: Recall the general pattern for heating any Group 2 nitrate: think what solid remains and which two gases are always released together.
walkthrough:
Remember the Group 2 nitrate pattern**
All Group 2 nitrates break up in the same way on heating. The solid nitrate becomes the solid metal oxide, and the nitrogen and extra oxygen leave as two gases, brown $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$. Nothing else is formed.

Balance for magnesium**
Start with one $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2$. That gives one $\text{MgO}$. The two nitrogens must give $2\text{NO}_2$. Count oxygens: 6 on the left, $1 + 4 = 5$ on the right so far, so you need $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$ to balance: $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \rightarrow \text{MgO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$.

hints: Compare the sizes of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ and think which ion has the higher charge density.
Think how a small, highly charging cation distorts the electron cloud of the large $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion and why that weakens the N-O bond.
walkthrough:
Picture the two cations side by side**
Both ions carry the same $2+$ charge, but $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is much smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ because magnesium is higher up Group 2 with fewer shells. Same charge packed into a smaller volume means $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has a much higher charge density and therefore a stronger polarising power.

See what the cation does to nitrate**
Imagine the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion sitting next to the cation. The intense positive field of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulls the electron cloud of the nitrate towards itself and distorts it far more than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ can. This polarisation weakens the N-O bonds within nitrate, so less heat is needed to break it apart into $\text{MgO}$, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$. That is why $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2$ decomposes at a lower temperature.

Final answer: compound that decomposes at a lower temperature: $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2$
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ / has higher charge density, so distorts / polarises the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion more, weakening it and making decomposition easier.

hints: Think of MgO as a base reacting with an acid: the metal forms the salt with the acid anion and the oxide oxygen ends up in another small product.
walkthrough:
Treat it as a simple base plus acid**
$\text{MgO}$ is a basic oxide. With dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ it undergoes neutralisation: $\text{MgO} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The soluble salt A is magnesium sulfate, $\text{MgSO}_4$, and water is the second product.

hints: Recall that dissolving involves breaking the lattice ($\Delta H_{latt}$) then hydrating the gaseous ions ($\Delta H_{hyd}$), so $\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$ in sign convention.

Compare $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ for the same $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ anion and decide which sulfate has the more exothermic lattice enthalpy and which has the more exothermic hydration enthalpy.
Think about which effect changes faster with cation size, the lattice term or the hydration term, and how that decides which $\Delta H_{sol}$ is more exothermic.
walkthrough:
Set up the energy cycle for dissolving**
Picture dissolving in two steps. First, split the solid into gaseous ions, which costs energy equal to $-\Delta H_{latt}$. Then surround each gaseous ion with water, which releases $\Delta H_{hyd}$. Overall: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$$ A more exothermic (more negative) $\Delta H_{sol}$ favours solubility.

Compare lattice and hydration for Mg versus Sr**
Both salts share the large $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ion, so the difference comes from the cation. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is far smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$. Smaller ions pack closer in the lattice and also attract water molecules more strongly. So $\text{MgSO}_4$ has a more exothermic $\Delta H_{latt}$ (harder to break) but also a more exothermic $\Delta H_{hyd}$ (more energy released on hydrating).

Decide which effect wins**
Here is the key A Level point. On going from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, both terms become less exothermic, but $\Delta H_{hyd}$ falls off faster because hydration depends very strongly on the cation radius, while the lattice contains the very large sulfate ion which dilutes the effect of changing the cation. The extra hydration energy released for the tiny $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ outweighs its extra lattice cost. Therefore $\text{MgSO}_4$ ends with the more exothermic $\Delta H_{sol}$ and dissolves readily, while $\text{SrSO}_4$ has a less favourable $\Delta H_{sol}$ and is insoluble.

Final answer: A is $\text{MgSO}_4$, B is $\text{SrSO}_4$.
$\text{MgSO}_4$ has a more exothermic $\Delta H_{latt}$ and a more exothermic $\Delta H_{hyd}$ than $\text{SrSO}_4$.
The difference in $\Delta H_{hyd}$ is greater than the difference in $\Delta H_{latt}$, so $\text{MgSO}_4$ has a more exothermic $\Delta H_{sol}$ and is more soluble.
